claims.claim: Francisco Franco died on 20 November 1975, ending nearly four decades of dictatorship; the transition to democracy that followed (Constitution ratified December 1978) dismantled the National-Catholic social order and opened the permissive climate in which Spanish youth culture, nightlife, and eventually Ibiza's club economy flourished.
claims.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Francisco Franco'
claims.note: Anchor date for the wing. The lane's thesis: rave's Spanish ground was prepared by the transition, not by any drug-specific liberalization alone.

claims.claim: La Movida madrilena was not merely tolerated but actively institutionalized by Madrid's Socialist city hall under Mayor Enrique Tierno Galvan: from 1983 the Ayuntamiento gave financial support to Movida publications and pop music, sponsored expositions, issued declarations of support, and folded Movida bands into official celebrations such as the San Isidro festivals — a state-embraced hedonist explosion unique in Western Europe.
claims.source: 'The Same in Name, But Different: the movida madrilena and the other movidas of Spain' (published scholarship, via ResearchGate)
claims.note: Tierno Galvan was mayor 15 May 1979 - 19 Jan 1986 (died in office). Scholarship frames city-hall sponsorship beginning 1983 as the institutionalization phase of the movement.

claims.claim: THE FLAGSHIP QUOTE, verified: Madrid mayor Enrique Tierno Galvan told the crowd 'Rockeros: el que no este colocado, que se coloque y al loro' at the III Gran Fiesta del Estudiante y la Radio ('24 Horas de Musica y Radio'), organized by RNE Radio 3's programme Tiempo de Universidad at the Palacio de los Deportes, Madrid, held on the Santo Tomas de Aquino student holiday, 28-29 January 1984 — reported in El Pais on 29 January 1984.
claims.source: El Pais, 29 January 1984 (article reproduced at the aplomez blog; broadcast footage held by Archivo RTVE, which labels it 'el concierto del Estudiante y la Radio de 1984')
claims.quote: Rockeros: el que no esté colocado, que se coloque y al loro
claims.note: Gloss: 'colocado' is slang for intoxicated/high; 'al loro' is Madrid slang for 'stay sharp/pay attention'. The popular rendering 'El que no este colocado, que se coloque... y al loro' drops the opening 'Rockeros:'; several retellings misplace the line at the San Isidro fiestas or a spring festival — the contemporaneous El Pais report and the RTVE archive footage (https://www.facebook.com/archivortve/videos/980665838672251/) fix it at the January 1984 student-radio festival. That an elected mayor said this from a city-embraced stage, to applause, is the lane's single best exhibit of official tolerance.

claims.claim: Spain never criminalized drug use or possession for personal use in its Penal Code: a 1974 Supreme Court doctrine held possession criminal only when intended for third-party consumption, and that position has been maintained ever since — so 'decriminalization' in Spain was a pre-existing condition, not a reform.
claims.source: Marta Valldaura, Silvie Ojeda, Agnes Rosell and Aura Roig, 'Spain's Decriminalisation: Decades of Quiet Innovation', TalkingDrugs, 6 March 2025
claims.quote: In 1974, the Spanish Supreme Court clarified that possession would only be criminal if intended for third-party consumption, exempting personal use from prosecution—a ruling maintained to this day.
claims.note: This is the legal bedrock under the whole lane: what Ibiza's dancefloors relied on was jurisprudence older than the transition, made socially operative by the post-Franco climate.

claims.claim: The 1983 reform of the Spanish penal code (the 'urgent and partial' reform enacted under the first Gonzalez government) did not legalize any drug, but it narrowed the definition of punishable conduct, reduced penalties, and introduced the distinction between substances causing serious harm to health (heroin, cocaine) and those not seriously harmful (cannabis) — consolidating the personal-use exemption in statute-era practice.
claims.source: OJP/NCJRS abstract of 'Present Spanish Drug Criminal Policy' in Drug Policies in Western Europe (Albrecht & van Kalmthout eds., 1989); see also TNI, 'Cannabis Regulation in Europe: Country Report Spain'
claims.note: No verbatim quote supplied: the OJP abstract text could not be captured verbatim on fetch (page rendered navigation only) — content stated per the abstract's summary and the TNI country report (https://www.tni.org/files/publication-downloads/cr_spain_final.pdf). A curator wanting the exact sentence should pull the NCJRS abstract directly.

claims.claim: The arc bent back in 1992: the Ley Organica 1/1992 de Proteccion de la Seguridad Ciudadana (the 'Ley Corcuera', 21 February 1992) made PUBLIC drug consumption and illicit possession — even when not intended for trafficking — a 'grave' administrative infraction punishable by fines (suspendable if the person entered accredited treatment), while private personal use remained outside criminal law. Public use was re-penalized by administrative sanction, not by crime.
claims.source: Boletin Oficial del Estado, BOE-A-1992-4252, Ley Organica 1/1992, art. 25.1
claims.quote: el consumo en lugares, vías, establecimientos o transportes públicos, así como la tenencia ilícita, aunque no estuviera destinada al tráfico, de drogas tóxicas, estupefacientes o sustancias psicotrópicas
claims.note: Art. 25.1 verbatim (statutory text via BOE). The law was politically explosive for its warrantless-entry 'patada en la puerta' clause, partially struck by the Constitutional Court in 1993 (see eldiario.es retrospective). Museum framing: Spain's permissive window for open public revelry was widest c. 1975-1992 — precisely the years Ibiza's open-air scene formed.

claims.claim: Through the 1980s Ibiza's flagship clubs ran open-air and all-night with no equivalent of UK licensing hours: DJ Alfredo Fiorito began his Amnesia residency in 1983 on an uncovered dancefloor under the trees, sets running to sunrise, while Ku in San Rafael drew crowds in the thousands around its open-air pool and stage.
claims.source: Kristan J Caryl, 'Celebrating 50 years of Amnesia, an Ibiza clubbing institution', DJ Mag, 4 June 2026
claims.quote: He was given his first Amnesia gig in 1983 and played under the trees that still stand, on the open-air dancefloor that is now covered.
claims.note: Corroborated by Amnesia's own history page (https://www.amnesia.es/en/history). The open-air, dawn-facing format is the material fact that Spain's legal climate made possible and that visiting Britons had no legal way to reproduce at home.

claims.claim: The permissive window closed physically in the early 1990s: stricter noise and licensing regulation in Ibiza forced the great open-air clubs to cover their dancefloors — Amnesia complied with a retractable roof over the Terrace — ending the island's uncovered all-night format even as its legend was being exported.
claims.source: Kristan J Caryl, 'Celebrating 50 years of Amnesia, an Ibiza clubbing institution', DJ Mag, 4 June 2026
claims.quote: The nineties brought stricter noise and licensing regulations to Ibiza. Amnesia acquiesced to municipal regulations with a new retractable roof over the Terrace.
claims.note: Neat periodization for the wing: Spain's 1992 public-order turn and Ibiza's early-90s roofing requirements are the same tightening seen at national and municipal scale.

claims.claim: 'Balearic beat' — the eclectic mid-1980s DJ style at the root of UK acid house — is literally named for the Balearic islands: the genre took its name from Ibiza, and its canonical author is Amnesia resident DJ Alfredo, whom the dance press titles the 'Father of the Balearic beat'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Balearic beat'; DJ Mag obituary 'DJ Alfredo, Ibiza legend and "Father of the Balearic beat", dies aged 71'
claims.quote: Balearic beat was named for its popularity among European nightclub and beach rave patrons on the Balearic island of Ibiza, a popular tourist destination.
claims.note: The strongest 'Ibiza named it' exhibit: the music itself carries the islands' name. DJ Mag obituary: https://djmag.com/news/dj-alfredo-ibiza-legend-and-father-of-balearic-beat-dies-aged-71

claims.claim: The founding story of UK rave, as told by its founders: in summer 1987 Paul Oakenfold, Danny Rampling, Nicky Holloway and Johnny Walker holidayed in Ibiza, heard Alfredo's sets at Amnesia, and on returning to London opened Shoom, Spectrum and The Trip — igniting acid house and the 1988 'Second Summer of Love'. This is why the dance press treats Ibiza as the spiritual home/birthplace of rave for much of the world.
claims.source: Told by the four DJs themselves and canonized in the dance press: Mixmag, '30 years on: The Summer Of Love continues to inspire us'; DJ Mag Alfredo obituary; retold across Ibiza histories
claims.note: Classified as lore deliberately: it is a participant-memoir origin myth, endlessly retold (Mixmag has commissioned a drama series, 'Ibiza87', on it) and broadly accurate in outline, but historians note acid house had multiple UK tributaries. Tellers: Oakenfold, Rampling, Holloway, Walker, as retold by Mixmag and DJ Mag.

claims.claim: The UK's legislative answer to what Spain had tolerated: the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, s.63, gave police powers to shut down open-air night gatherings of 100 or more people with amplified music, and wrote rave's musical form into criminal statute with a definition of 'music' aimed at electronic dance records.
claims.source: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, s.63 (as enacted), legislation.gov.uk
claims.quote: "music" includes sounds wholly or predominantly characterised by the emission of a succession of repetitive beats
claims.note: s.63(1)(b) verbatim. The wing's hinge contrast: in 1984 a Spanish mayor blessed the party from the stage; ten years later the British Parliament defined its beat in order to ban it. Royal assent 3 November 1994.

claims.claim: Published scholarship draws the comparison explicitly: of all countries, the UK took the most drastic legal measures against raving, criminalizing it outright in 1994 — the pole against which Spain's administrative-fine, never-criminal-in-private tradition stands at the opposite end.
claims.source: Aljona Altuhhova, 'Raving (worldwide)', Global Informality Project (UCL)
claims.quote: The most drastic legal measures against raving were taken in the UK, where raves were criminalised by being included in the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act in 1994.
claims.note: The entry does not itself discuss Spain; the Spain side of the contrast is carried by the BOE/TalkingDrugs claims above. For the wall text, pair this sentence with LO 1/1992 art. 25.1: statute-book crime versus administrative fine is the documented legal contrast.

verdicts.claim: Franco died 20 November 1975 ending nearly four decades of dictatorship; the transition (Constitution ratified December 1978) dismantled the National-Catholic order and opened the permissive climate in which Spanish youth culture, nightlife, and Ibiza's club economy flourished [Britannica, 'Francisco Franco']
verdicts.evidence: Direct fetch of britannica.com/biography/Francisco-Franco returned HTTP 403, but a domain-restricted search of britannica.com surfaced the article's own text: Franco 'died November 20, 1975, in Madrid,' was 'head of the government of Spain until 1973 and head of state until his death in 1975' (dictatorship 1939-1975, i.e. ~36 years), and 'After Franco's death on November 20, 1975, the accession of Juan Carlos as king opened a new era, which culminated in the peaceful transition to democracy.' Nothing retrieved from the cited source mentions the December 1978 Constitution, 'National-Catholic social order,' youth culture, nightlife, or Ibiza.
verdicts.correction: The death date, dictatorship length, and transition to democracy are supported by the cited Britannica article. But the source does not support the second half as attributed: it does not mention the Constitution's December 1978 ratification (true — referendum 6 Dec 1978 — but needing a different citation), nor anything about dismantling the National-Catholic order, permissive nightlife, or Ibiza's club economy. Trim the claim to what Britannica states, or cite additional sources for the youth-culture/Ibiza causal chain.

verdicts.claim: La Movida madrilena was actively institutionalized by Madrid's Socialist city hall under Tierno Galvan: from 1983 the Ayuntamiento financially supported Movida publications and pop music, sponsored expositions, issued declarations of support, and folded Movida bands into official San Isidro celebrations — unique in Western Europe ["The Same in Name, But Different", via ResearchGate]
verdicts.evidence: The cited ResearchGate page (publication 270819825) returned HTTP 403 on fetch, and multiple searches found no accessible full-text mirror (only the same RG link plus context pages); the paper's specific passages could not be checked. Reachable secondary corroboration is much weaker than the claim: Wikipedia's La Movida Madrileña article says only 'the government under socialist mayor Enrique Tierno Galván had a more open approach regarding the movement, and subsidized various artistic endeavours,' and press coverage notes he revived San Isidro festivities with youth music concerts. Nothing reachable supports 'from 1983,' 'declarations of support,' financial support to Movida publications specifically, or the 'unique in Western Europe' superlative.
verdicts.correction: Source unreachable — per lane rules this defaults to unsupported. The general direction (Tierno Galván's city hall subsidized Movida-era arts and put youth/pop concerts into San Isidro) is corroborated in reachable sources, but the specific package (1983 start date, publications funding, expositions, declarations, 'unique in Western Europe') rests entirely on a paywalled/blocked source and should not run in the caption as verified until someone with access confirms the passages.

verdicts.claim: Tierno Galvan said 'Rockeros: el que no este colocado, que se coloque y al loro' at the III Gran Fiesta del Estudiante y la Radio ('24 Horas de Musica y Radio'), organized by RNE Radio 3's 'Tiempo de Universidad' at the Palacio de los Deportes, Madrid, on the Santo Tomas de Aquino student holiday, 28-29 January 1984; reported in El Pais 29 January 1984; RTVE archive labels the footage 'el concierto del Estudiante y la Radio de 1984'
verdicts.evidence: The aplomez blog (aplomez.blogspot.com/2013/10/recitales-de-ayer.html) reproduces the El País article dated 29 January 1984, which opens: "'Rockeros: el que no esté colocado, que se coloque y al loro'. El consejo del alcalde de Madrid, Enrique Tierno, fue seguido durante toda la jornada de ayer por los cientos de jóvenes que abarrotaron el Palacio de los Deportes..." — exact quote wording, venue, dates 28-29 Jan 1984, and organizer RNE-Radio 3's 'Tiempo de Universidad' (directed by Fernando Segundo) all confirmed. The Archivo RTVE label is also confirmed: an Archivo RTVE Facebook video is captioned 'este momentazo de Enrique Tierno Galván en el concierto del Estudiante y la Radio de 1984.'
verdicts.correction: Two details are not in the cited source: (1) the 1984 El País text gives the event no edition number and never uses 'Gran' — it is called '24 Horas de Música y Radio' / 'Fiesta del Estudiante y la Radio'; 'III' is only an inference from the blog's 1985 follow-up being called the 'IV Fiesta del Estudiante y la Radio.' Drop 'III Gran' or source it separately. (2) The 'Santo Tomás de Aquino student holiday' framing appears nowhere in the reproduced article — cut it or find a source. Everything else, including the flagship quote verbatim and the RTVE archive label, checks out.

verdicts.claim: Spain never criminalized drug use or possession for personal use in its Penal Code; a 1974 Supreme Court doctrine held possession criminal only when intended for third-party consumption, maintained ever since [TalkingDrugs, Valldaura/Ojeda/Rosell/Roig, 6 March 2025]
verdicts.evidence: Fetched talkingdrugs.org/spains-decriminalisation-decades-of-quiet-innovation/: authors Marta Valldaura, Silvie Ojeda, Agnés Rosell, Aura Roig; published 6 March 2025. The article contains the flagged quote verbatim: 'In 1974, the Spanish Supreme Court clarified that possession would only be criminal if intended for third-party consumption, exempting personal use from prosecution—a ruling maintained to this day.' It also states: 'Spain never undertook a formal process of decriminalisation; drug use and possession for personal use were simply never criminalised in its Penal Code.' The claim's characterization of decriminalization as a pre-existing condition, not a reform, matches the source (which does note administrative penalties exist for public consumption).

claims.claim: MDMA first appears in Merck's records in 1912 under the lab-journal name 'Methylsafrylamin', inside German patent application No. 274 350 filed 24 December 1912 — a procedural patent in which MDMA was only an unnamed intermediate on an alternative route to hydrastinine, a styptic (haemostatic). It was never the product.
claims.source: Bernschneider-Reif S, Oexler F, Freudenmann RW, 'The origin of MDMA (Ecstasy) — separating the facts from the myth', Pharmazie 61 (2006) 966–972 (Merck Corporate History archive study)
claims.quote: Merck applied for this patent to protect an alternative chemical method for synthesizing the styptic hydrastinine, not appetite suppressants.
claims.note: Text verified verbatim from the PDF. Nuance for the label copy: hydrastinine is a clot-PROMOTING styptic, so even the common 'anticoagulant program' shorthand is backwards — the archive papers say haemostatic.

claims.claim: The famous 'Merck made MDMA in 1912 as an appetite suppressant' story is a myth. Freudenmann, Öxler and Bernschneider-Reif examined Merck's Darmstadt archive (Addiction 101:1241–1245, 2006): no appetite-suppressant program existed at Merck 1900–1960, and MDMA was not pharmacologically tested at all until 1927, when Dr. Max Oberlin ran the first tests looking for adrenaline/ephetonine-like substances — work halted for economic reasons.
claims.source: Freudenmann RW, Öxler F, Bernschneider-Reif S, 'The origin of MDMA (ecstasy) revisited: the true story reconstructed from the original documents', Addiction 101(9):1241–1245 (2006); companion paper Pharmazie 61 (2006) 966–972
claims.quote: Archive documents revealed that Merck's scientists did not perform basic pharmacological tests with MDMA (now called "Safrylmethylamin") before 1927.
claims.note: Quote verified verbatim from the Pharmazie companion PDF. The paper attributes the myth's spread to uncritical copy-paste citation in later literature.

claims.claim: Alexander Shulgin did not invent MDMA but reintroduced it: he re-synthesized and self-tested it in September 1976, passed it in 1977 to Oakland psychotherapist Leo Zeff, and in 1978 published with David E. Nichols the first report of its human psychopharmacology — the paper trail behind his erroneous 'father of MDMA' title.
claims.source: Passie T, 'The early use of MDMA (Ecstasy) in psychotherapy (1977–1985)', Drug Science, Policy and Law 4 (2018); Benzenhöfer U & Passie T, 'Rediscovering MDMA (ecstasy): the role of the American chemist Alexander T. Shulgin', Addiction 105(8) (2010)
claims.quote: In 1977, Shulgin introduced Zeff to MDMA, which looked like a better and less toxic MDA.
claims.note: Quote verified verbatim from the open-access Passie 2018 paper.

claims.claim: The quiet therapeutic era, 1977–1985: published scholarship estimates only a few dozen therapists used MDMA in psychotherapy before scheduling, with Leo Zeff alone estimated to have introduced it to thousands of clients; George Greer and Requa Tolbert treated 80+ patients 1980–1985 and published the era's main clinical account.
claims.source: Passie T, Drug Science, Policy and Law 4 (2018)
claims.quote: a few dozen therapists used MDMA in a psychotherapeutic setting between 1978 and 1985
claims.note: The therapy community's code name 'Adam' is Zeff-era tradition — told in memoir (Myron Stolaroff, The Secret Chief, 1997, about Zeff) and repeated in the scholarly reviews; the naming story itself is memoir-grade, not archive-grade.

claims.claim: The street name 'ecstasy' dates to circa 1981, chosen by a Los Angeles distribution network purely as marketing: the distributor, quoted anonymously in Bruce Eisner's Ecstasy: The MDMA Story (1989), said it would sell better than the more accurate 'Empathy'.
claims.source: Unnamed distributor quoted in Bruce Eisner, Ecstasy: The MDMA Story (Ronin, 1989); carried in David Pearce, 'Utopian Pharmacology', hedweb.com
claims.quote: it would sell better than calling it 'Empathy'
claims.note: Lore because the teller is an anonymous trafficker interviewed by Eisner — a memoir chain, not a document. The 1981/LA framing is Eisner's.

claims.claim: The DEA placed MDMA in Schedule I using its emergency scheduling power for the first time ever: the notice was published in the Federal Register on 31 May 1985 (50 FR 23118), and the control took effect on 1 July 1985 — the July 1 date is confirmed in the notice's own EFFECTIVE DATE line.
claims.source: Federal Register, Vol. 50, No. 105, May 31, 1985, p. 23118 (DEA, Schedules of Controlled Substances: Temporary Placement of MDMA in Schedule I); scan hosted by Wikimedia Commons; hearing archive at MAPS
claims.quote: EFFECTIVE DATE: On July 1, 1985, MDMA will be subject to Schedule I control.
claims.note: Quote extracted verbatim from the Federal Register scan (US government work, public domain). The 1984–1988 administrative law judge hearings over permanent scheduling are archived at maps.org/research-archive/dea-mdma/.

claims.claim: At Dallas's Starck Club (opened 12 May 1984, interior by Philippe Starck), ecstasy was sold openly across the bar while still legal — by bartenders and via the cigarette girl — a trade the club's oral history attributes to individual employees, not management. Dallas police made America's first ecstasy-possession arrest days after scheduling, and the DEA raided the club on 7 August 1986.
claims.source: Oral history 'Nightclubbing: Starck Club', Red Bull Music Academy Daily (2016) — tellers named: resident DJ Kerry Jaggers, owner Blake Woodall, GM Greg McCone, Mark Ridlen, David Muir, Wade Hampton, Michael Cain, Molly Emerson
claims.quote: It was sold over the counter by bartenders
claims.note: Filed as lore: the open-sale detail is participant memoir. The opening date, raid date and first-arrest claim are the article's documented anchors.

claims.claim: The Texas supply story: former seminarian Michael Clegg's 'Texas Group' mass-distributed MDMA in Dallas before the ban — the DEA's own figure, as reported, put his distribution at upwards of half a million pills a month — and Texas political pressure (Sen. Lloyd Bentsen is the name told in the club histories) helped trigger the 1985 emergency action.
claims.source: Texas Monthly, 'When Dallas Led the Party Drug Revolution, He Was Its Ecstasy King'; DEA figure as reported in Red Bull Music Academy Daily 'Nightclubbing: Starck Club' (2016)
claims.quote: distributing upwards of 500,000 pills a month in Dallas at the time
claims.note: Quote verbatim from the RBMA piece, which attributes the figure to the DEA. The Bentsen detail circulates in the club retellings; treat that name as reported journalism, not a verified primary document.

claims.claim: Botanical ancestry, encyclopedic fact only: safrole — the principal component of sassafras oil (from Sassafras albidum) and of Brazilian Ocotea pretiosa oil — is the classic historically documented precursor family associated with MDMA, and for that reason is internationally controlled as a listed precursor.
claims.source: Encyclopedic: Wikipedia 'Safrole' (CC BY-SA), reflecting the UN 1988 Convention Table I listing and DEA List I chemical status
claims.quote: Safrole is listed as a Table I precursor under the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances.
claims.note: MUSEUM POLICY: named strictly as ancestry and regulation. No process, quantity, or method detail exists in this claim and none may be added at exhibit level.

claims.claim: How ecstasy reached Ibiza in the mid-1980s: the standard histories point to the Bhagwan Rajneesh sannyasin network — Matthew Collin's Altered State documents that the movement popularized ecstasy and built distribution channels beyond the US, and by the mid-80s sannyasin-linked centres and club workers were present on Ibiza — but the specific island-arrival story remains anecdotal; David Hillier's investigation concluded there is no smoking gun.
claims.source: Matthew Collin, Altered State: The Story of Ecstasy Culture and Acid House (Serpent's Tail, 1997); tested in David Hillier, 'Did the Cult From Wild Wild Country Introduce MDMA to Ibiza?', Vice (2018) — tellers: Collin, plus Hillier's interviewees (Tony D'Andrea, 'Maria', 'Terrence', Stephen Armstrong)
claims.quote: set in place distribution systems that would result in its dissemination beyond the United States
claims.note: Quote is Collin (Altered State) as excerpted in the Vice piece. Filed as lore because Hillier, checking the claim, found the Ibiza leg anecdotal.

claims.claim: The 1987 Amnesia summer, the scene's founding legend: four London DJs — Paul Oakenfold (his 24th-birthday trip), Danny Rampling, Nicky Holloway and Johnny Walker — took ecstasy at Amnesia under DJ Alfredo's open-genre Balearic sets, and on returning founded Shoom, Spectrum/Future and The Trip, seeding UK acid house. Per Collin's Altered State the printed story first appeared in i-D in May 1988 (the 'Amnesiacs'), and historians note it is a selective myth — London arrived at house 'a year after the Midlands and North' (Sheryl Garratt).
claims.source: Simon Reynolds, Energy Flash (1998); Matthew Collin, Altered State (1997); historiography examined in 'How much of UK dance music history is real?', DJ Mag longread — tellers: the four DJs themselves, via i-D May 1988
claims.quote: this take on how acid house fever spread first appeared in i-D in May 1988
claims.note: Quote verbatim from the DJ Mag longread, which is citing Collin's Altered State. The trip happened; its status as THE origin of acid house is the lore part, and both standard histories frame it as legend-with-a-kernel.

claims.claim: The molecule's other documented life: MAPS's phase-3 program (MAPP1, published Nature Medicine 2021; MAPP2, 2023) met primary endpoints for MDMA-assisted therapy in PTSD, but on 4 June 2024 an FDA advisory committee voted against approval, and on 9 August 2024 the FDA issued Lykos Therapeutics a Complete Response Letter requiring an additional phase-3 trial. The FDA published the CRL itself on 4 September 2025. As of 2026 MDMA remains unapproved; the research arc continues.
claims.source: Lykos Therapeutics press release, 'Lykos Therapeutics Announces Complete Response Letter for Midomafetamine Capsules for PTSD' (PR Newswire, Aug 2024); MAPS statement on FDA's public release of the CRL (Sept 4, 2025)
claims.note: Companion source: https://maps.org/2025/09/04/fda-public-release-of-crl/ — the advisory committee's June 4, 2024 vote cited data-reliability questions; the CRL's stated remedy is a further phase-3 trial.

verdicts.claim: MDMA first appears in Merck's records in 1912 under the lab-journal name 'Methylsafrylamin', inside German patent application No. 274 350 filed 24 December 1912 — a procedural patent in which MDMA was only an unnamed intermediate on an alternative route to hydrastinine, a styptic (haemostatic). It was never the product.
verdicts.evidence: Source reached: WebFetch returned the Pharmazie PDF as raw binary; extracted locally with pypdf (7 pages, 33,755 chars). Header confirms the citation exactly: 'The origin of MDMA ("Ecstasy") - separating the facts from the myth / S. Bernschneider-Reif(1), F. Oxler(1), R. W. Freudenmann(2) ... Pharmazie 61: 966-972 (2006)', first author at 'Merck Corporate History, Merck KGaA, Darmstadt'. Every element checks out. Abstract: 'MDMA was in fact mentioned for the first time in files from 1912, but not under this name. In the lab journals it was called "Methylsafrylamin". In a patent certificate it was mentioned only with its chemical structure.' The supplied quote is a verbatim, unaltered match to the abstract: 'Merck applied for this patent to protect an alternative chemical method for synthesizing the styptic hydrastinine, not appetite suppressants. MDMA was not the key substance in this patent, only a precursor.' Patent number and filing date, from the body: 'The first and more important patent with the No. 274 350 is entitled "Darstellung von Alkyloxyaryl-, Dialkyloxyaryl- und Alkylendioxyarylaminopropanen bzw. deren am Stickstoff monoalkylierten Derivaten". It was assigned to the company E. Merck by the German Imperial Patent Office in Berlin. It started on December 24, 1912, when the patent application was filed. It is a procedural patent for...' — confirming 'procedural patent' and 24 December 1912. 'Unnamed intermediate' confirmed twice: 'A thorough analysis of the patent specification No. 274 350 showed that MDMA was not the purpose of the patent. It was mentioned only as a by-product and chemical intermediate in one the pathways which started from safrole' and 'In the patent specification MDMA appeared as a chemical formula and not under the name "MDMA"'. 'Never the product' confirmed: 'The patents and also all other archive documents did not provide any evidence of a specific pharmacological interest in the precursor MDMA or of plans to create an anorectic. Obviously, it was never intended for sale.' One nuance worth flagging for label copy, though it does not make the claim wrong (the claim quotes the abstract's own wording): the body specifies the immediate synthetic target as the hydrastinine analog 3-methyl-hydrastinine, not hydrastinine itself — 'Dr. Walter Beckh (1870-1915) and his co-worker Dr. Otto Wolfes (1895-1942) came up with the idea to synthesize and use 3-methyl-hydrastinine as a replacement for hydrastinine... In the newly developed synthetic pathway to 3-methyl-hydrastinine MDMA was mentioned as one of several key precursors under the name of "Methylsafrylamin". Importantly, the company was interested in the new styptic 3-methyl-hydrastinine, not the precursor MDMA.' Also confirmed incidentally: the second, related patent is No. 279 194.

verdicts.claim: The 'Merck made MDMA in 1912 as an appetite suppressant' story is a myth; no appetite-suppressant program existed at Merck 1900-1960, and MDMA was not pharmacologically tested at all until 1927, when Dr. Max Oberlin ran the first tests looking for adrenaline/ephetonine-like substances — work halted for economic reasons.
verdicts.evidence: Both cited papers reached and each element is supported. Addiction 101(9):1241-1245 (2006), authors and pagination confirmed as stated. Its abstract: 'There were no indications for plans to develop an appetite suppressant at Merck between 1900 and 1960'; 'Although MDMA was, in fact, first synthesized at Merck in 1912, it was not tested pharmacologically because it was only an unimportant precursor in a new synthesis for haemostatic substances'; 'In 1927 and 1959, the pharmacological effects of MDMA were studied at Merck, but not in humans.' The Oberlin specifics and the 'economic reasons' halt come from the companion Pharmazie paper the claim also cites, body text: 'In 1927 -- the procedural patent was about to expire that year -- Dr. Max Oberlin (1896-?) at Merck resumed the work in this field. He was looking for new substances with adrenaline-like or ephetonine-like effects. MDMA has a structure similar to ephetonine (Merck launched this synthetic ephedrinum in 1927)... The files from 1927 (not 1912) were the first indications for pharmacological tests with MDMA at Merck... Research on the substance was stopped for economic reasons and the substance was buried in oblivion for some decades.' The supplied quote is verbatim from the Pharmazie abstract (not the Addiction abstract, but the claim's source line does cite the Pharmazie companion): 'Archive documents revealed that Merck's scientists did not perform basic pharmacological tests with MDMA (now called "Safrylmethylamin") before 1927. These tests were halted for economic reasons.' Two wording notes, neither changing the verdict: (a) the archive finding is phrased as 'no indications for plans to develop an appetite suppressant', marginally weaker than the claim's 'no appetite-suppressant program existed'; (b) Pharmazie footnote 20 identifies the likely root of the myth, useful for the label — 'Most probably this rumor is based on confusing MDMA with MDA. The latter, and not MDMA, was tested for its anorectic effects by Smith Kline French in the 1950s.' The paper separately debunks the related WWI-soldiers story: 'Statements in the literature saying that the synthesis of MDMA in 1912 was intended for soldiers in World War I are false.'

verdicts.claim: Alexander Shulgin did not invent MDMA but reintroduced it: he re-synthesized and self-tested it in September 1976, passed it in 1977 to Oakland psychotherapist Leo Zeff, and in 1978 published with David E. Nichols the first report of its human psychopharmacology — the paper trail behind his erroneous 'father of MDMA' title.
verdicts.evidence: Confirmed, but note the sourcing split: the URL listed first (Passie 2018, SAGE) supports only the Zeff hand-off — 'In 1977, Shulgin introduced Zeff to MDMA, which looked like a better and less toxic MDA', matching the supplied quote verbatim. It contains no mention of September 1976, no mention of a 1978 Shulgin/Nichols publication, and does not discuss the 'father of MDMA' attribution. Every remaining element is supported, in near-identical wording, by the companion source the claim also cites — Benzenhofer U & Passie T, 'Rediscovering MDMA (ecstasy): the role of the American chemist Alexander T. Shulgin', Addiction 105(8):1355-61 (2010), PMID 20653618, DOI 10.1111/j.1360-0443.2010.02948.x (abstract retrieved verbatim via PubMed): 'Alexander T. Shulgin is widely thought of as the "father" of +/-3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA). This paper re-assesses his role... In the mid-1970s Shulgin learned of a "special effect" caused by MDMA, whereupon he re-synthesized it and tried it himself in September 1976, as confirmed by his laboratory notebook. In 1977 he gave MDMA to Leo Zeff PhD, who used it as an adjunct to psychotherapy and introduced it to other psychotherapists. Shulgin was not the first to synthesize MDMA, but he played an important role in its history... the fact that in 1978 he published with David Nichols the first paper on the pharmacological action of MDMA in humans, explains why Shulgin is sometimes (erroneously) called the "father" of MDMA.' That last sentence supports the claim's 'erroneous' framing in the source's own word. One detail is true but comes from neither cited source: 'Oakland' is not stated by Passie 2018 (which places only 'the majority of these therapists' in California) nor by the 2010 abstract (which says only 'Leo Zeff PhD'); independent reference sources do document Zeff as an Oakland psychologist with an office on Telegraph Avenue, so the descriptor is accurate — it simply needs a different citation if a label asserts it. Also per the 2010 abstract, PIHKAL's 1965 synthesis claim is reported as Shulgin's own account and he 'did not try it' then, which is consistent with the claim's 'did not invent MDMA but reintroduced it'.

verdicts.claim: The quiet therapeutic era, 1977-1985: published scholarship estimates only a few dozen therapists used MDMA in psychotherapy before scheduling, with Leo Zeff alone estimated to have introduced it to thousands of clients; George Greer and Requa Tolbert treated 80+ patients 1980-1985 and published the era's main clinical account.
verdicts.correction: Three of the four elements are exact; the fourth is not supported as stated. Greer and Tolbert did not publish 'the era's main clinical account' — Passie never ranks their work that way, describes their reports as self-published in 1983 and 'later published in the Journal of Psychoactive Drugs' where they became 'classics in the field', and names contemporaries with substantially larger caseloads, which undercuts 'main' if it is read as largest or most representative: Deborah Harlow 'conducted MDMA-assisted psychotherapy with more than 200 clients before 1985' and Rick Ingrasci 'treated 100 patients in about 150 sessions from 1980 to 1985'. Suggested label wording: '...treated over 80 patients between 1980 and 1985; their published reports became classics of the era's clinical literature.' Secondary precision note: the 'few dozen' estimate is bracketed 1978-1985 in the source, not 1977-1985 (the 1977 in the claim's heading matches the article's title range, so the heading itself is fine, but the estimate should not be described as covering 1977).
verdicts.evidence: Passie T, 'The early use of MDMA ("Ecstasy") in psychotherapy (1977-1985)', Drug Science, Policy and Law (2018), full text reached at the cited SAGE URL. The supplied quote is verbatim and correctly framed as an estimate: 'An estimate from the relatively poor data available in the literature, supported by information provided personally to the author, is that a few dozen therapists used MDMA in a psychotherapeutic setting between 1978 and 1985.' Zeff: 'During the next 12 years, Zeff administered MDMA to about 4000 people and trained more than 150 therapists' — 'thousands of clients' is accurate, and note the source's figure is people dosed, distinct from the 150+ therapists he trained. Greer/Tolbert: 'During the 1980-1985 period, Greer, together with his wife Requa Tolbert, a registered psychiatric nurse, treated over 80 patients with MDMA-assisted psychotherapy' — '80+' and the 1980-1985 range are exact. Only the 'main clinical account' characterization fails: the source's own words are 'classics in the field', and it lists Harlow (200+ clients) and Ingrasci (100 patients) alongside them.
